summary: This RFC describes the DCN protocols for keeping connectivity, routing, and clock information in a local network. It was published as an example that designers and implementers of other local networks might find useful.

eli5.summary: A group of computers in one building keeps checking who is nearby, who knows the best path, and what time it is. This note explains how they do it.

questions: what are the dcn local network protocols
how does dcn handle routing and clock information
what is the dcn hello protocol
how does dcn calculate roundtrip delay
subtitle: How DCN Fuzzball local networks find neighbors, pick minimum-delay routes and keep their clocks in step.

tldr.problem: A set of randomly connected personal computers and service hosts needs connectivity, routing and timekeeping without a central controller.
tldr.mechanism: Neighboring hosts exchange HELLO messages (IP protocol number 63) that carry delay and clock-offset tables. Each host measures roundtrip delay, adds it to what neighbors report and routes via the minimum-delay path, while also adjusting its clock.
tldr.outcome: The RFC was published as an example for designers and implementers of other local networks. It is for local nets of up to 256 hosts and is not meant for large, complex networks.

today: RFC 891 is listed as an Internet Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes the DCN protocols as they were in December 1983.

sections.title: The DCN Local Network
sections.content:
RFC 891 describes the local-net architecture and protocols of the Distributed Computer Network (DCN), a family of local nets built on Internet technology and a PDP11-based software implementation called the Fuzzball. The RFC says DCN nets had been in operation for about three years, including clones in the USA, UK, Norway and West Germany.

The design philosophy is to put complete functionality in every host, which can act as packet switch, gateway and service host at once. Hosts joined by a haphazard collection of serial, parallel and contention-bus interfaces organize themselves into a network with routing based on minimum delay. The architecture is meant for up to 256 hosts and gateways, and the RFC states it is not for large, complex networks and does not support the sophisticated routing of, for example, the ARPANET.
sections.eli5: A small group of computers in one place work out by themselves how to reach each other and what time it is, with no boss computer.

sections.title: Hosts, Net Table and Host Table
sections.content:
Each DCN physical host runs several processes, each with a unique 8-bit port ID. Each internet process supports a virtual host with a unique 8-bit host ID. A host ID is formed from a chosen octet of the Internet address plus an offset, so addresses and host IDs correspond one to one.

Routing uses two tables in every host. The Host Table is indexed by host ID. It holds roundtrip delay, logical-clock offset, the port ID of the outgoing process, a TTL and an update timestamp, and says which link leads to each local virtual host. The Net Table lists neighbor nets and gives the host ID of the gateway to each. The table ends with an entry whose net fields are zero: if its Hops field is under 255, its gateway is used for all other nets, and if it is 255 all unlisted nets appear unreachable.

The Host Table is kept up to date by HELLO messages. The Net Table is fixed at configuration time unless the host runs a GGP/EGP gateway process, which maintains it. Operators can also change entries.
sections.eli5: Every computer keeps two lists: one saying which road leads to each neighbor in the room, and one saying which doorway leads to each other building.

sections.title: The HELLO Message
sections.content:
A HELLO message is an IP datagram carrying the reserved protocol number 63. It has a fixed area with a checksum, the date, the time, a timestamp, an address offset and the number of hosts. A host area follows with a delay and an offset for each host, copied from the sender's Host Table.

There are two formats. A host sending to another host on the same local net sends both areas, and all other HELLOs carry only the fixed area. The fields are byte-swapped relative to the ordinary PDP11 representation.
sections.eli5: A HELLO is a short note to a neighbor saying who I am, what time I think it is and how far away I think everyone is.

sections.title: Delay Measurement and Route Updates
sections.content:
Each host sends HELLOs to its neighbor on every shared link and keeps state for each link. The roundtrip delay is computed from timestamps echoed back in the next HELLO. The calculation does not depend on clock offsets at either host and works even when a neighbor simply forwards the HELLO back unchanged, as ARPANET IMPs and broadcast nets do. It is performed only if the lengths of the last sent and received HELLOs match.

When a valid delay is computed, the host adds it to each delay in the HELLO and compares the results with its Host Table. An entry is updated if the link is already the entry's output link. It is also updated if a different link offers a delay lower by at least the switching threshold (currently 100 milliseconds). Updates for hosts on foreign nets use the roundtrip delay. A delay above the maximum (currently 30 seconds) marks the host as down. Delays below the minimum (currently 100 milliseconds) are rounded up to it, so on low-delay links the algorithm degenerates to minimum hops.

When a host is declared down, updates are ignored while its TTL counts down, giving time for the bad news to spread and preventing routing loops. A sender also reports the maximum delay for any host it reaches over the link the HELLO is sent on, which avoids potential loops.

The clock offset is learned the same way: the difference between the HELLO's Time field and the local clock plus half the roundtrip delay, added to the neighbor's reported offset.
sections.eli5: Neighbors time how long a note takes to go back and forth. Each computer picks the neighbor with the shortest total trip. It only switches if the new road is clearly faster, so it does not keep changing its mind.

sections.title: Timeouts and Parameters
sections.content:
A Host Table TTL is set to 120 seconds on each update and decremented once a second. If it reaches zero without another update, the virtual host is declared down. The 120 seconds allows at least four HELLOs from every neighbor, because the maximum gap between HELLOs is 30 seconds on the slowest link (1200 bps).

The HELLO interval is generally 16 times the expected roundtrip time for the longest packet on that link, ranging from about eight to 30 seconds. IP datagram time-to-live is set to 30, so the maximum delay on any path is 30 seconds. The specification suggests a keep-alive of four HELLO intervals.
sections.eli5: If you do not hear from a neighbor for two minutes, you assume they are gone. The notes go out often enough that you would normally get several in that time.

sections.title: Clocks and the Formal Processes
sections.content:
The formal specification describes three processes: CLOCK, HELLO and HOST. The CLOCK process keeps a physical clock, an apparent clock used by clients and an actual clock from an outside reference. They run at 1000 Hz and are reset at midnight UT. A neighbor's time is used to correct the local clock only if the sender is the designated master clock host and its date is marked valid.

Corrections are slewed gradually rather than applied as steps, so the apparent time is smoothed. A suggested adjust fraction of seven gives a maximum slew rate of less than 2 milliseconds per second for a 1000-Hz clock. A large correction is stepped instead, and it starts a HOLD interval during which timestamps are invalid and delay calculations are suppressed. The HOST process runs once a second to decrement TTLs and start a hold-down cycle when a host goes down.
sections.eli5: Each computer's clock is nudged a tiny bit at a time toward the right time, so it never jumps. If it is badly wrong it jumps once and waits a while before trusting any time notes.

sections.title: Link-Level Framing (Appendix)
sections.content: The appendix describes how an Internet datagram is carried on each kind of link. On program-interrupt serial links the data is framed with DLE-STX and DLE-ETX, and any DLE in the data is sent doubled, a character-stuffing scheme with no checksum. DDCMP links place the datagram unmodified in the frame's Data field. HDLC and X.25 LAPB links use bit stuffing, with a zero inserted after five one bits. ARPANET 1822 links add a 96-bit leader when connected to an IMP, gateway or Port Expander. Ethernet frames use type 0800 hex for IP and 0806 hex for ARP, and ARP maps Ethernet addresses to Internet addresses.

viz.caption: HOW A HOST UPDATES ITS ROUTES

items.title: Measure
items.text: Compute roundtrip delay from echoed timestamps.

items.title: Add
items.text: Add that delay to each delay in the neighbor's HELLO.

items.title: Compare
items.text: Switch only if the new path is better by the switching threshold.

items.title: Expire
items.text: Count TTL down and declare silent hosts down.
